chapters.title: Chapter 4: The Post-2008 and Post-COVID Regimes

lessons.title: 2021-22 Global Inflation: Supply Chains, Stimulus, and the Return of Inflation Fear

children.text: A shipping container that typically cost around $1,500 to move from China to the US West Coast was, at points in 2021, being quoted at well over $10,000, and on some routes reportedly above $20,000. That single, absurd number captures the 2021-22 inflation episode better than any single CPI print: a world where money was abundant, but the physical machinery of getting goods from factory to shelf had partially broken down.

body.text: The 2021-22 episode is the rare case where you can watch all three engines from Chapter 1 fire at once, in sequence: demand-pull from unprecedented stimulus, cost-push from broken supply chains and then a war, layered on top of the fastest expansion of money and credit most of the world had seen in decades.

events.title: Unprecedented Stimulus
events.description: Facing COVID lockdowns, the Fed cuts rates near zero and launches open-ended bond buying, while the US government passes trillions of dollars in fiscal relief. Other major economies respond on a similar scale.

events.title: Supply Chains Break, "Transitory" Is the Word
events.description: Goods demand surges while factories, ports and shipping remain disrupted. Inflation starts climbing through the year, and the Fed and most central banks initially call it "transitory", expected to fade as supply chains normalise.

events.title: The Fed Retires "Transitory"
events.description: Fed Chair Jerome Powell tells Congress it is time to retire the word "transitory", a public acknowledgment that the inflation was proving far more persistent than initially assumed.

events.title: Russia Invades Ukraine
events.description: A fresh, entirely separate cost-push shock hits an already-inflating world: energy prices spike, particularly in Europe, and global food and fertilizer prices surge, since Russia and Ukraine together account for a large share of global wheat and sunflower oil exports.

events.title: Inflation Peaks Globally
events.description: US CPI inflation peaks at 9.1% in June 2022, a 40-year high. The UK and eurozone see similarly historic peaks. India's CPI breaches the RBI's 6% upper tolerance band for most of the year, touching close to 7.8% in April, the subject of the next lesson.

children.text: Stimulus at a Scale Never Seen

The US alone passed multiple rounds of fiscal relief through 2020 and 2021, widely cited as totalling more than $5 trillion combined, while the Fed simultaneously cut rates to near zero and bought bonds on an open-ended basis. This is demand-pull and monetary engines firing together: households and businesses had more spending power than usual (demand-pull), financed substantially by newly created central bank money and cheap credit (monetary), echoing the M x V = P x Q dynamic from Chapter 2, just without the collapse in confidence that turned Weimar's version into a true hyperinflation.

children.text: Supply Chains Break, Demand Shifts Sideways

Lockdowns kept people out of restaurants, cinemas and flights, but they still had income to spend, so demand shifted hard toward physical goods: home electronics, furniture, exercise equipment. Factories, ports and shipping lines, many still operating under pandemic restrictions, could not scale up fast enough. A global shortage of semiconductor chips hit auto production particularly hard, leaving finished cars stuck half-built for months. This is the cost-push engine, but unlike a single oil shock, it was spread unevenly across dozens of different goods categories at once, which is part of why it took so long for policymakers to agree on how persistent it would actually be.

body.title: Trace the Regime Through Its Stages
body.scenario: Consider three snapshots: (1) mid-2020, when stimulus cheques and near-zero interest rates were flowing through the US economy but goods were still generally available, (2) mid-2021, when container costs had spiked and chip shortages were emptying car lots, but the war in Ukraine had not yet happened, and (3) mid-2022, with energy and food prices spiking globally alongside everything else.
body.prompt: Using the three engines from Chapter 1, identify which engine (or engines) is most dominant at each of these three stages, and explain why treating this whole episode as a single, unchanging "regime" would have made it harder to read correctly in real time.
body.modelAnswer: Stage one is primarily demand-pull and monetary: spending power was up sharply, financed by stimulus and near-zero rates, while supply was not yet the binding constraint. Stage two is dominated by cost-push: supply chains, not demand, had become the bottleneck, container costs and chip shortages were squeezing output regardless of how much people wanted to buy. Stage three adds a second, distinct cost-push shock, the war's impact on energy and food, on top of the first two. Treating this as one static regime would have been a mistake, because the correct policy response, and the correct assets to hold, differ by stage: cooling demand helps in stage one, but does very little to fix a physical shipping bottleneck in stage two or a war-driven energy shock in stage three. Reading which engine is dominant right now, not applying a single label to the whole episode, is exactly the skill this course has been building.

children.text: Recall the callout at the end of the 1970s lesson: the word "transitory" makes economists nervous because the 1973 oil shock also looked transitory at first, right up until a wage-price spiral made it structural. History nearly repeated the framing, if not the full mechanism. Through most of 2021, the Fed and other central banks described the inflation surge as transitory, expected to fade once supply chains normalised. By late November 2021, with inflation still climbing and showing signs of broadening beyond the original supply-constrained categories, Fed Chair Jerome Powell publicly said it was time to retire the word.

body.text: This is a genuine test of the Chapter 1 regime-shift checklist, applied to the most recent episode in this course. Core inflation trending up for multiple quarters, input prices (shipping, chips, raw materials) running far ahead of normal, and inflation expectations climbing were all visible through mid-to-late 2021, well before the Fed's own language caught up. The toolkit from the start of this course was not just historical trivia; it would have flagged this shift early.

children.text: Then a War: The Russia-Ukraine Shock

Russia's invasion of Ukraine on 24 February 2022 added a second, entirely separate cost-push shock on top of the first. Europe, heavily reliant on Russian natural gas, saw energy prices spike sharply. Russia and Ukraine together account for a large share of the world's wheat and sunflower oil exports, so global food and edible oil prices jumped as well, a shock India, a major edible oil importer, felt directly through its own food inflation. Russia is also a major fertilizer exporter, so the disruption fed into future harvests too, not just current shipments. Two unrelated shocks, a pandemic supply-chain breakdown and a war, landed on the same global economy within about a year of each other.

body.title: Quick Check
body.question: Why is the 2021-22 inflation episode a useful case study for the entire framework built across this course, rather than a single clean example of one engine?
options: Because it was caused purely by a single central bank's mistake
Because it shows all three engines, demand-pull, cost-push and monetary, contributing at different stages, requiring the observer to track which one is dominant as the episode evolves
Because inflation stayed exactly the same in every country throughout the episode
Because it had no connection to central bank policy at all
body.explanation: Unlike a clean single-engine case like the 1973 oil shock or Weimar's pure monetary collapse, 2021-22 blended stimulus-driven demand-pull and monetary expansion with two distinct cost-push shocks, pandemic supply chains and then the war, arriving in sequence. Reading it well requires tracking which engine dominates at each stage, not applying one label to the whole episode.

points: The 2021-22 inflation surge combined all three engines from Chapter 1: demand-pull and monetary expansion from unprecedented COVID-era stimulus, then cost-push from broken supply chains, then a second cost-push shock from the Russia-Ukraine war.

The Fed's initial "transitory" framing echoed the same mistake that made the 1973 oil shock harder to fight; the word was formally retired in late November 2021 as the data made the persistence clear.

US CPI peaked at a 40-year high of 9.1% in June 2022, with the UK and eurozone seeing similarly historic peaks, confirming this was a genuinely global shock rather than a single country's policy failure.
India's CPI breached the RBI's 6% tolerance band through most of 2022, touching close to 7.8% in April, driven by a mix of the same global pressures and domestic factors covered in the next lesson.

The regime-shift checklist from Chapter 1 could have flagged this shift months before central banks' own language caught up, the clearest demonstration yet of why that toolkit matters in real time, not just in historical hindsight.
